results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.summary: The MDS 2015 criteria define clinically established PD as bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity, in the absence of absolute exclusion criteria, with two or more supportive features. A clear and dramatic levodopa response is one of the strongest supportive criteria. The tremor-dominant subtype tends to have a more benign motor course.
results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease

results.authors: Tolosa E, Wenning G, Poewe W
results.summary: Rest tremor, asymmetric onset, associated bradykinesia, rigidity, hypomimia, and abnormal DaTscan are features that distinguish Parkinson disease from essential tremor. Essential tremor is typically bilateral, postural or kinetic, and DaTscan is normal. Family history of tremor is common in ET but may also occur in familial PD; clinical examination features remain the primary differentiating tool.
results.title: Distinguishing Essential Tremor from Tremor-Dominant Parkinson Disease

results.authors: Gray R, Ives N, Rick C, et al.
results.summary: Levodopa-based therapy provided superior patient-rated quality of life and mobility compared to dopamine agonists or MAO-B inhibitors as initial PD therapy, with no significant difference in long-term motor complications at 7-year follow-up.
results.title: PD MED: A Large Randomised Trial of Initial Treatment in Parkinson Disease

output.summary: MDS 2015 criteria require bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity; a clear levodopa response is a key supportive criterion. The tremor-dominant PD subtype is associated with a generally better prognosis than the postural-instability-gait-difficulty (PIGD) subtype. Family history of tremor alone does not diagnose essential tremor; the character of tremor (rest vs postural/kinetic), asymmetry, and presence of bradykinesia are the critical distinguishing features. DaTscan is abnormal in PD and normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism. Levodopa remains the most effective initial therapy across age groups.

key_clinical_evidence: The 4–5 Hz left-hand rest tremor that diminishes with purposeful use and re-emerges at rest is the cardinal feature distinguishing tremor-dominant PD from essential tremor, where tremor is predominantly postural and kinetic

Family history of maternal hand tremor is a red herring: ET and PD are distinct conditions; co-occurrence of asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and hypomimia cannot be explained by familial ET
DaTscan laterality is mandatory: the presynaptic dopaminergic deficit must be contralateral to the clinically worse side — left-worse signs correspond to reduced RIGHT putaminal uptake

Straightforward diagnosis is supported by the complete cardinal triad (left-side-predominant bradykinesia, rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity), non-motor prodromal features (hyposmia, constipation), and absence of atypical red flags (no vertical gaze palsy, no early falls, no cerebellar signs, no severe early dysautonomia)

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Eleanor Voss is a 71-year-old right-handed retired school librarian presenting to the neurology outpatient clinic with her husband, Richard, for evaluation of a progressive left hand tremor and generalized slowing over the past two years. She first noticed a subtle intermittent shaking in her left hand approximately two and a half years ago while seated reading in the evenings. She initially attributed the tremor to fatigue or stress, and a neighbor suggested it might be 'the same tremor that runs in the family' — her mother had had shaky hands for many years and was never formally diagnosed. Over the past 18 months the tremor became more persistent and obvious, particularly when her hands were resting in her lap or on the armrests of a chair. Her husband first noticed it clearly during a church service when her left hand was trembling on her knee. Importantly, she notes the shaking virtually disappears when she reaches for objects or is using her hand purposefully, and returns once the hand is again at rest. She has not noticed that the tremor responds to alcohol.

Over the past year she has developed progressive slowing of her left hand in daily tasks. Fastening buttons on her blouse with her left hand has become difficult, she has stopped using left-handed scissors, and her handwriting has become progressively smaller and harder to read. Her husband has noticed she takes noticeably longer to get ready in the morning and that her left arm does not swing when she walks. She describes a pervasive stiffness in the left arm and shoulder, initially attributed to arthritis, but persistent despite conservative measures. Over the past six months she has noticed a change in her gait: shorter steps and a slight forward lean. She has not fallen but felt unsteady turning quickly in the kitchen on one occasion three months ago. Her voice has become softer and her husband frequently asks her to repeat herself. She has also noticed progressive difficulty with her sense of smell for approximately two years, blaming sinus issues. Constipation has developed over the past 18 months, requiring a fiber supplement daily. She denies vivid dreams, acting out dreams, visual hallucinations, cognitive complaints, or urinary incontinence. Sleep is otherwise reportedly adequate. There are no symptoms suggestive of orthostatic lightheadedness, syncope, or cerebellar dysfunction. She is on no medications that could cause or worsen parkinsonism. She has severe longstanding claustrophobia and declined brain MRI despite preparation; she also declined sedation but agreed to non-contrast CT.
